Laboratory-reared cohorts of Neanthes arenaceodentata were monitored from the moment of egg fertilisation to track early developmental traits. Upon hatching, the trochophore larvae that emerged from the gelatinous egg masses were characterised by a remarkably minimal body mass, with newly hatched individuals weighing approximately 0.0000082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000082 grams]. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the species’ reliance on planktotrophic larval development, where early feeding immediately after yolk absorption is critical for sustaining growth. The age at birth was recorded in the same experimental group, with larvae first observed swimming freely 1.5 days [ab = 1.5 days] following egg fertilisation, a brief embryonic period typical of nereidid polychaetes developing in warm, stable conditions. The rapid transition from the fertilised ovum to a free-swimming trochophore stage underscores the accelerated developmental pace characteristic of this opportunistic species, which thrives in disturbed sedimentary habitats where early dispersal confers a significant survival advantage.

As the growing juveniles transitioned into the benthic phase, their somatic growth trajectories were assessed across multiple replicate containers maintained at a controlled water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Under these stable thermal conditions, the time since birth at puberty was observed to be 52 days since birth [tp = 52 days since birth], representing the period from hatching to the first macroscopic signs of gonadal development in the coelomic cavity at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This relatively brief interval to the onset of gametogenesis suggests that Neanthes arenaceodentata prioritises early reproductive investment over prolonged somatic growth, a life-history strategy commonly observed in polychaetes inhabiting ephemeral or anthropogenically enriched environments. The recorded age at puberty aligns well with published accounts for congeneric species, although slight inter-cohort variation of several days was noted, likely attributable to minor differences in food availability during the critical juvenile growth period.

The maximum recorded body mass attained by reproductively active adult individuals in these laboratory populations was 0.060 grams [Wwi = 0.060 grams], an ultimate wet weight achieved well after the onset of reproductive activity. This asymptotic mass was typically reached several weeks following the puberty threshold and was maintained with only minor fluctuations during the reproductive lifespan of the individual. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty was substantially lower, with sexually maturing worms measuring approximately 0.018 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.018 grams] at the time when the first signs of gametogenesis became microscopically evident. The threefold increase in body mass between the pubertal stage and the attainment of maximum adult size indicates a sustained period of somatic investment concurrent with early reproductive bouts, a pattern that distinguishes this nereidid from species exhibiting a more discrete separation between growth and reproduction.

Longevity records for this species under controlled laboratory settings were derived from a dedicated survivorship experiment. Individuals held at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] exhibited a maximum lifespan of 160 days [am = 160 days], a duration that encompasses the entire post-embryonic existence from the hatching of the trochophore to the natural death of senescent adults. This lifespan is notably compressed compared to many other polychaete species of similar adult body size, reflecting the semelparous or iteroparous-with-short-lifespan reproductive strategy that has been proposed for Neanthes arenaceodentata in environments with high predation or physical disturbance. Post-reproductive mortality typically accelerated sharply after the final spawning events, with most individuals failing to survive beyond the 160-day benchmark, indicating a clear physiological coupling between reproductive effort and somatic senescence.

From an ecological and comparative perspective, the life-history traits of Neanthes arenaceodentata illustrate a coordinated suite of fast-paced demographic parameters shaped by its role as a pioneering coloniser of organically enriched sediments. The brief age at birth of 1.5 days [ab = 1.5 days] and the early pubertal timing of 52 days since birth [tp = 52 days since birth] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] together allow rapid population turnover and quick numerical response to resource pulses. The threefold mass gain from the 0.018 gram [Wwp = 0.018 gram] pubertal body mass to the 0.060 gram [Wwi = 0.060 gram] adult maximum indicates that a substantial fraction of assimilated energy continues to be channelled into somatic growth during the early reproductive window. The complete lifespan of 160 days [am = 160 days] caps this fast cycle, ensuring that multiple generations can occupy a single disturbance event within a single annual cycle, reinforcing the species’ ecological dominance in dynamic coastal soft-sediment habitats at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
